newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK inflation jump points to rate rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK inflation jump points to rate rise.

text.p: British inflation leapt above the government's target in June, making an interest rate rise at this week's Bank of England meeting look a near certainty.

The Office for National Statistics said on Tuesday headline inflation rose to 2.9 percent in June from an annual rate of 2.6 percent in May. Underlying inflation, which excludes mortgage interest payments and is the targeted measure for the central bank, rose to 2.7 percent from 2.5 percent in May.
The data was a shock for financial markets which expected underlying inflation to stay steady at 2.5 percent, bang in line with the official target.
Shares and government bond prices slumped as the odds of an interest rate rise shortened dramatically. The pound soared to new highs at 2.9730/40 marks for the same reason.
Gilt futures traded on the LIFFE exchange slipped 9/32 to 114-15 on the figures before recovering to 114-20. The FTSE index of 100 leading shares fell to 4,786, down 25 from the opening.
City economists said the inflation data made a rate rise later this week almost inevitable.

"This is a disappointing set of figures. The market might eventually take some comfort from the fact seasonal food prices have lifted the figure in a fairly dramatic way, but they still point in a direction of a rate rise," said Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International.
Seasonal food prices rocketed by five percent in June but they are notoriously volatile. The main upward pressure on the RPI index came from rises in housing costs and motoring costs.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown raised petrol duties in his first budget but did little else to rein in buoyant consumer spending while two interest rates since Labour stormed to power on May 1 have forced mortgage rates higher.

The Bank of England, newly empowered to set interest rates, starts its monthly meeting on Wednesday to discuss monetary policy and is widely expected to raise the 6.5 percent base rate at midday on Thursday.

The central bank raised rates by a quarter point in June in an attempt to cool robust consumer demand and stem price pressures. But economists said the small number of tax rises aimed at consumers in last week's budget, coupled with the latest inflation data, mean another monetary tightening is on the cards.
A Reuters poll of economists conducted after last week's budget found that 21 out of 24 economists forecast a rate rise at the meeting with most expecting a quarter-point rise.

Brown raised the overall tax burden by almost 6 billion pounds ($10 billion) in the budget, but with around 90 percent of these measures aimed at the corporate sector many households escaped with their finances unscathed. ($ = 0.594 British Pounds)
